facts.text: A tolerance, or acceptance band, is the allowed disagreement between simulation and physical test before a model is judged inadequate for the decision it supports.
facts.quote: A tolerance, or acceptance band, is the amount of disagreement between simulation and physical test that is allowed before the model is judged not good enough for the decision it supports.

facts.text: A simulation acceptance band must be derived from the decision the model supports, rather than chosen for convenience.
facts.quote: the acceptance band is derived from the decision, not chosen for convenience.

facts.text: No framework prescribes a universal simulation-to-test tolerance.
facts.quote: No framework prescribes a universal simulation-to-test tolerance.

facts.text: The aviation seat guidance's 10% criteria are application-specific, not a universal simulation-to-test tolerance.
facts.quote: The aviation seat guidance's 10% criteria are application-specific.

facts.text: The European automated-vehicle regulation requires manufacturers to set and document their own simulation-to-test thresholds for each model.
facts.quote: The European automated-vehicle regulation requires manufacturers to set and document their own thresholds for each model

facts.text: The United Nations car braking regulation leaves simulation-to-test thresholds to the manufacturer's documented method, with the authority's agreement.
facts.quote: the United Nations car braking regulation leaves them to the manufacturer's documented method with the authority's agreement.

facts.text: No published tolerance for an off-road automatic-braking model was found.
facts.quote: No published tolerance for an off-road automatic-braking model was found [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Euro NCAP's virtual-testing protocol requires at least 75% of verification tests in a scenario cluster to meet the qualification criteria.
facts.quote: Euro NCAP's virtual-testing protocol gives a related rule: at least 75% of the verification tests in a scenario cluster must meet the qualification criteria

facts.text: Several numeric tolerances in Euro NCAP's virtual-testing protocol are still bracketed as unconfirmed.
facts.quote: several of its numeric tolerances are still bracketed as unconfirmed [Chapter 3].

facts.text: The booklet recommends deriving the simulation acceptance band from the safety margin and measurement uncertainty.
facts.quote: The booklet's design principle is to derive the band from the safety margin and the measurement uncertainty.

facts.text: If the risk area in the mining standard leaves X meters of margin, combined model-form, numerical and input uncertainty must be demonstrably smaller than X.
facts.quote: If the risk area in the mining standard leaves X meters of margin, then model-form, numerical and input uncertainty together must be demonstrably smaller than X.

facts.text: A model accuracy criterion is not a system safety criterion: an imperfect model can still be conservative enough to support a decision.
facts.quote: a model accuracy criterion is not a system safety criterion: a model can be imperfect yet conservative enough for a decision

facts.text: A model with low average error can still be dangerously optimistic at the collision boundary.
facts.quote: have low average error while being dangerously optimistic at the collision boundary.

facts.text: The simulation acceptance band must be set before results are seen and cannot be changed after inconvenient findings.
facts.quote: The band is set before results are seen, so it cannot be changed after inconvenient findings [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Measurement uncertainty can limit testing of a simulation acceptance band: ground truth for object position, relative speed, intervention timing and stopping distance must be more precise than the discrepancy being measured, or the band cannot be tested.
facts.quote: ground truth for object position, relative speed, intervention timing and stopping distance must be more precise than the discrepancy being measured, or the band cannot be tested at all [Chapter 10].
